title: Narrowing and Type Guards
summary: Narrowing means checking a value so TypeScript can learn more about its type.
introduction: Narrowing means checking a value so TypeScript can learn more about its type. A value might be text or a number. Check which kind it is before you use an action that only works for one of those kinds.
learningObjectives: Narrow a union with typeof, equality checks, in and instanceof
Model variants as a discriminated union and make a switch exhaustive with never
Write a type predicate and explain why non-null assertions and casts are risky

blocks.text: The compiler tracks each check you write. After `if (value === null) return`, the type of `value` no longer includes `null`; inside `if (typeof value === "number")` it is `number`; and whatever is left after those branches is the remaining member, here `string`. No annotations, just ordinary JavaScript conditions.

blocks.title: typeof.ts

rows: Values created by `new Dog()` or a subclass
The member of a discriminated union with that literal

blocks.text: When several object shapes share a property with a different literal type in each (`kind: "circle"`, `kind: "square"`), a `switch` on that property narrows to the matching shape in every `case`. The `default` branch assigns the value to a variable of type `never`: if every case is handled, nothing reaches it and the assignment is fine. Add a new member to the union and forget a case, and the assignment fails with a message naming the shape you forgot.

blocks.title: shapes.ts
npx tsc shapes.ts
blocks.content:
shapes.ts:13:13 - error TS2322: Type '{ kind: "rect"; width: number; height: number; }' is not assignable to type 'never'.

13       const unreachable: never = shape;
               ~~~~~~~~~~~


Found 1 error in shapes.ts:13

blocks.text: This is the compile-time safety net that makes discriminated unions so valuable in large codebases: every `switch` over the union is re-checked whenever the union grows. Add the missing case and the file compiles.

blocks.title: shapes-fixed.ts

blocks.text: `instanceof` narrows class instances. `in` narrows by the presence of a property, which suits interfaces that have no runtime class. When a check is too complex for the compiler to follow, or you want to reuse it, wrap it in a function whose return type is a *type predicate*: `animal is Fish` tells the compiler that a `true` result proves the argument is a `Fish`. Since TypeScript 5.5 the compiler even infers predicates for simple arrow functions, which is why `filter((v) => v !== null)` below produces a `string[]`.

blocks.title: guards.ts

blocks.text: `swimmers` is typed `Fish[]` because `filter` has an overload that accepts a type predicate, and `strings` is `string[]`. A type predicate is a promise: if `isFish` returned `true` for a bird, the compiler would believe it. Keep predicate bodies simple and honest.

Narrowing also catches comparisons that can never be true. Comparing a `Status` with a string that is not one of its members is almost always a typo, and the compiler says so instead of letting the branch silently never run.

blocks.title: overlap.ts
npx tsc overlap.ts
blocks.content:
overlap.ts:4:10 - error TS2367: This comparison appears to be unintentional because the types 'Status' and '"finished"' have no overlap.

4   return status === "finished";
           ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~


Found 1 error in overlap.ts:4

blocks.text: Two pieces of syntax let you skip narrowing. The non-null assertion `value!` removes `null` and `undefined` from a type, and a type assertion `value as Type` replaces the type altogether. Neither generates a check; both are you telling the compiler to stop looking.

blocks.title: nonnull.ts
npx tsx nonnull.ts (compiles cleanly, then crashes)
blocks.content: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'toFixed')

blocks.title: Common mistake: silencing the compiler with ! or as
blocks.text: `Map.get` returns `number | undefined` because the key may be absent, and `!` threw that information away. The honest version is `const price = prices.get("pencil"); if (price === undefined) { ... }` or `prices.get("pencil") ?? 0`. Likewise `response as User` does not validate a response; it only changes what the editor believes. Use `as` for the few cases where you know more than the compiler can (narrowing a DOM element you just created, for instance) and never to make an error go away.

blocks.title: satisfies, the safe cousin of as
blocks.text: `const config = { port: 3000 } satisfies Config` checks the literal against `Config` without changing its inferred type, so you keep the precise literal types and still get the error if a property is wrong. It is the right tool when you want validation of a literal rather than a conversion.

questions.question: In an exhaustive `switch` over a discriminated union, why is the `default` branch given `const unreachable: never = shape;`?
questions.explanation: If every member has a case, shape is narrowed to never in default and the assignment is valid. When a member is missing, its type remains and the assignment fails, pointing at the forgotten case.
options: To throw a runtime error for unknown shapes
To make the compiler report any union member that has no case
To convert the shape to a string for logging
Because switch statements must end with an assignment

questions.question: `user!.name` inserts a runtime check that throws a clear error when `user` is null.
questions.explanation: The non-null assertion is erased at compile time. If user is null at runtime, the property access throws the usual TypeError, exactly as it would without the !.

seo.description: Learn TypeScript narrowing: typeof, in and instanceof guards, discriminated unions with exhaustive never checks, type predicates, and why ! and as hide bugs.
